I love the synchronicity of this puzzle running the day I watched Mike Krukow retire from the broadcast booth in San Francisco. Especially because there was a magic 63-across GIANT in there. Baseball clues are the reason I have loved crosswords for the past 35 years, because my grandma would ask 10-year-old me for help with the sports clues. As a vegetarian who enjoys jackfruit and a Giants fan who loves Kruk:  “Grab some pine, meat!”

The well-researched article on home runs covered all the bases.

(It was batter than expected.)

I knew exactly zero theme answer starters to refer to home runs; i.e., jack wasn't the only thing I didn't know. 

Baseball is the only spectator sport I've watched a fair amount of on TV and have attended a few games in person. (How I got some very nice photos of Barry Bonds.) But none of that experienced help me here.

To be so dumbfounded by a Monday puzzle is a rare experience for me. Thank you, Sam, for spelling it out.

For years, I paid individually for various Times subscriptions to avoid one thin dime of my money going to sports. I detest the lingo, the violence, the sexism, the gambling, all of it. I cannot express how much I resent sports emphasis in word puzzles intended for a general audience. There are so many subjects covered in these puzzles about which I know nothing, about which I enjoy learning. Sports will never be one. Please keep these for your niche game areas and spare the rest of us.

For an Australian who’d somehow come across “Leadoff batter” as describing a particular role in baseball , (c.p.”Opener” in cricket) LEADOFF HOMERUN caused no problems. The other theme clues all came as straightforward themeless. (Although I cannot recall, in 70 years, having ever seen TATER TOTS). BOMB and BLAST, I can easily grasp as describing home runs.It would be interesting to hear the stories behind the other two, Jack is at the edge of my comprehension, TATERTOTS ????
But then, it would probably leave most Americans,and indeed most non-followers of cricket if i said of a fielder that they are in the gully.

Obviously the theme was a huge mystery to me, so the puzzle solved like a themeless, and I had to rely on crosses to get quite a few entries.

I've only recently encountered JACKFRUIT for the first time - there was a piece on it in The Guardian, how it generally is quite tasteless unless you prepare it right. I just looked it up and learned it has very little protein - why would it be a *meat* replacement then? Apparently in Polish it's called "owoc chlebowca" ("fruit of the bread tree") and it's only sold as a snack: I saw a packet of dried jackfruit strips it at the supermarket last week.

Poor Midge URE, who never became known enough in the US to be a clue for the NYT crossword, although he was very popular in his native UK in the 1970s and 1980s.  

He's probably best known in the US for producing and co-writing with Bob Geldof the song, "Do They Know It's Christmas?," which inspired other charity records such as "We Are the World."

Fun puzzle, and an appropriate level of challenge for a Monday. Today I learned that, like many of the commercial or cultural items I and many Boomers had assumed had been around forever, Tater Tots have only been around for as long as we have. 1953 in the case of Tots. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tater_tots I still don't recall them coming up in popular culture (not counting the ubiquitous casserole recipes) until Napoleon Dynamite. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tater_tots
The answer ALL TIED suggests that only one side could be tied.

Well now, that’s a tight theme.  I mean, what kind of theme answer could you get with “dinger”, say?  

Speaking of which, that revealer lands perfectly.  

I think the cluing was perfect for Monday, where there was just enough non-obvious to get the brain involved, in general.  In other words, instead asking for the opposite of “white”, say, today the puzzle asked for the opposite of “liability”.  

Plus, there was the grinner, with the BANANA/ARROW quote, and a trio of lovely answers in HAVOC, MOTIFS, and BOX SET.

Good to see you again, Helen, after a four-year absence.  This was a lovely way to LEAD OFF the week.  Thank you!

Good timing for a baseball-themed puzzle as yesterday the Ottawa Titans defeated the Evansville (Indiana) Otters to win the Frontier League Championship. While Ottawa used to have a AAA baseball team, now the Frontier League is as high-level as baseball gets in this city. 

I've never heard of JACK or TATER to mean a home run, but then I am not a huge baseball person. I thought the cluing of "Dugout, e.g." in a baseball-themed puzzle was a little bit devious. Like Sam, I got it only from the crosses.

Maybe I'm the only one who thinks EELY is nonsense and has no place as an answer.  INURN too, though I saw another comment about that .  

Everything else was fine, but those were shoehorned in my book.

OFF TOPIC

Recently I have been working my way through some of the more challenging puzzles in the archives. Today I came across a puzzle that really floored me, and I thought I would pass on the recommendation. It is Sunday, January 30, 2005. 

I don't want to say too much about it, but I found it to be both challenging and ingenious in its conception. I have a feeling it is probably quite renowned among the serious puzzle community, but it was a real discovery for me. I hope that others will appreciate it as well.

While wait for Mr. Baseball to comment, I too have heard it used for the first batter in any inning, but the clue hews to the "official" meaning of the term. https://www.baseball-reference.com/bullpen/Leadoff_home_runs_leaders

@Bill in Yokohama I've also heard it used both ways, but apparently baseball keeps track of the "first batter up in the game for either side" as an official stat, so we have this: https://www.mlb.com/news/most-career-leadoff-home-runs-in-mlb-history So technically, the term only refers to the first inning, but I have to concur with Barry here that both usages are common. The clue is correct in any case.
@Matt However, if you were to say "Shohei Ohtani leads the league in leadoff home runs this year," it would be understood to mean in the first inning only.

@Bill in Yokohama
But the clue is for 38A + 41A – i.e., LEADOFF HOMERUN. That stat refers to a first-inning only event.  George Springer, who probably played his last career game yesterday for the Jays is, I believe, 3rd on the all-time list for lead-off home runs.

@Muzzy

First of all, I do respect how you feel and I'm also not a huge sports person either. I actually have a lot of issues with big money sports. This was absolutely not a favorite theme of mine.

But how many sports puzzles, that are seriously like kind of all about sports are there!? Not a lot.

Once in awhile there's a Star Trek themed puzzle, which I'm over the moon about, and others aren't, so what if sometimes there's a sports puzzle!? 

You didn't even need to know the sports stuff to solve this particular puzzle. 

There have been themes about Mario Brothers, Shawshank Redemption, escape rooms, art, etc etc ..  

Not every puzzle is going to resonate with each of us individually.  And that is completely okay!! I mean, if you hate all the puzzles, that's one thing, but if you occasionally hate a puzzle because it has too many sports references, then just move on to the next day.

@HeathieJ The lovely thing is, there is an appropriate place for sports themed puzzles, called the Athletic, which I avoid for obvious reasons. That is where this puzzle belongs. Star Trek never caused CTE, Mario Brothers don't encourage gambling, escape rooms don't encourage doping. Sports are a cesspool I would rather avoid, and lucky us, the Times has a place just for that purpose.

@Muzzy

You *do* realize sport is one of the few things the average person actually knows quite a bit about, right? A sports one is exactly the kind of theme best suited for a general audience. Now, vindictive hatred of all sports, that's quite niche indeed. Do you really believe you're in the majority here?

@Muzzy

not sure if you're a real person when you say 'I can't express how much I resent sports etc etc' you are expressing your feelings. take a chill pill and learn a few new words - thankfully Will & CO as I like to think of the crossword team at the Times doesn't force too much sports and arcane trivia into our heads.  words with meaning that are not slang and insider talk are always best.

@Muzzy 

Star Trek and video games in excess may never have caused CTE but they have been the instruments of stunted social skills and even incelism for many.  And an overindulgence in escape rooms may cause escape-room brain. 

My point:  feel free to hate what you like. 

But don’t expect others to alter their likes and behaviors based on your aversion. 

Any pursuit that presents potential harm only to the individual pursuing it is perfectly acceptable to this libertarian.

@Muzzy

you think the amorphous concept of "sports" benefited financially from this puzzle?

@muzzy

Your hatred of sports due to gambling, CTE, etc… are valid reasons why you avoid them. Unfortunately big money industries will have corruption, and things like injuries are going to go hand and hand with sports. But you can say that about any of the other big industries. Should there never be a movie theme because of the rampant sexual assault in Hollywood? Or if you use Mario as an example should video games be excluded because call of duty promotes violence and can cause addiction (esports has its own plethora of issues). Is it all sports? Track and field? Or only the ones that you have deemed unworthy of being enjoyed?

@Muzzy

You won’t get a lot of agreement here, but you’re absolutely right. It’s annoying how much useless sports knowledge I’ve accumulated from these puzzles. No idea how people could get excited to watch the same game over and over for their whole lives, never mind the ethical issues of supporting brutal, brain-damaging sports like football or boxing.

@Patrick J.

Only TATER is used for a home run.  Supposedly derived from "long tater" to describe a larger than normal potato when the game was more of a rural pastime.  Search engine says it got a boost in popularity in the 60s.

If Tater Tots haven't made their way down under, be thankful. This is from Wikipedia:
"Tater tots are grated potato formed into small cylinders and deep-fried, often served as a side dish."

@Al  in Pittsburgh

Tater tots are tasty! They won't ever replace French fries for me, but can be a fun alternative on occasion. Think marshmallow-shaped latkes: finger food easily dipped into any variety of savory sauce. (My preferred dipping sauce being a paprika aioli.)

How the Polish chlebowiec relates to whatever tree breadfruit grows on, I have no idea.

@Matt

Why would a season end in September, of all months? The weather is still fine for outdoor sports, people are generally back from holiday - isn't this the perfect time for the season to go on?

@Andrzej 

Consider the country/continent as a whole, young Jedi. 

In cities from Seattle to Chicago, from Milwaukee to Toronto and on to Boston and even New York…winter is coming. 

It’s autumn. It’s getting cold. Baseball’s rhythms are warm-weather and picnic rhythms.  It’s green grass, leafy trees and warm breezes. 

The post-season will occupy all October and maybe even a bit of November.  You’ll not infrequently see snow in the post-season, depending on who’s playing.
@Andrzej It is indeed - October baseball is a "thing" here

@Matt

This is so confusing! I'm further North than all of the US except Alaska, and October is usually still outdoor weather. Also, what on earth is the post-season? Apparently baseball games are still on? But if so, why are you sad that the season is over?

@Andrzej There was a time when the baseball season ended at the end of September or very early October. The most exciting moment in all of baseball history (indeed, in all sports) was the Shot Heard Round the World, October 3, 1951, the last game of a three-game playoff that decided the National League tie between the Giants and the Dodgers. https://youtu.be/lrI7dVj90zs?si=U_arGFq_zJC7PLhi Now, to attract more viewers, Major League Baseball has added multiple rounds of playoffs, so the World Series doesn't end until late October, or sometimes even November. Hence, for most teams, the season is over.

@Andrzej The playoffs can run through October and occasionally into early November. So the regular season is over, but a dozen teams are in the playoffs, culminating in the World Series (yes, I know…”world”), which starts October 23.

@Joe 

In fairness the moniker World Series is increasingly accurate as the best players in the world, from all over the world, play in the Majors.

@Matt

The saddest day only if your team didn't make the playoffs.

@Joe

The name "World Series," and even its erstwhile alternate version, "World's Series," predates the internationalization of the sport.  It was first used in 1903, when the champions of the National and American Leagues, then competitors, not part of a unified organization, met for the first time.

(Side note, MLB as we know it has only existed since 2000, although the phrase "major league baseball" is much older.)

For generations, even after baseball was introduced to other lands, nearly all the best players were Americans.  (The most egregious omissions were not foreign players, but rather Black Americans, who had to play in the separate Negro Leagues.)

Today, even still, most experts put the Japanese and maybe Korean leagues at AAA level in the US, the Mexican League at AA, and so on.  

But the World Series IS international.  Toronto was in it last year, and the last time I looked, it was on the other side of Lake Ontario.  Yes, Lake Ontario.

@J I doubt you're the only one. But let's make a distinction between "nonsense" and simply words that are less common in real life than in crosswords. Crossword constructors need to use words with common letters more often than their normal frequency because they work with potential crossing words, and may be the best way to populate a particular section of a puzzle. These words are commonly called "crosswordese." EELY is an example of this, but it's a real word: https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/eely Similarly, INURN is a legitimate word, too: https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/inurn If you're new to crosswords, it's understandable that you might be indignant about rare words being used on a supposedly easy day, but hopefully, you'll get more used to how words are chosen for the puzzles. If you're not new to crosswords, you're just stubborn, as words like these have been used since Day 1, and aren't going anywhere.
